title: The Score Can Be Right, but the Story May Be Wrong
author: Jane R. Shore
summary: Jane R. Shore opens with the eighteenth-century moral panic over reading fever to note how completely the worry has flipped: today we fear young people cannot stay absorbed in books at all. She accepts that the PISA 2025 reading decline is real, a 25-point OECD average drop roughly equal to a year of learning, but argues that the story attached to the scores is less certain than the scores themselves. Treating reading as an assessment construct with boundaries, she coins construct lag for the gap between what tests hold still and how young people's information lives are changing. Shore makes three moves: the story itself is changing as reading blends with searching and comparing across media, understanding may be visible in forms other than text, and PISA's own questionnaire data show rising belonging even as curiosity weakened. She ends by asking what human capacities schools develop that headlines leave out.
points: Average reading performance across 35 OECD countries fell 25 points between 2018 and 2025, about a year of learning.
PISA timing data showed students struggling with longer texts and answering quickly rather than reading carefully.
Shore uses a decathlon analogy: the score is real but depends on which events count.
When nearly every ability must pass through text to be assessed, schools risk privileging the medium over the meaning.
PISA found 76 percent of students felt they belonged at school, a finding that barely registered in headlines.
quotes: Two centuries later, the pendulum has fully swung. This time, we are no longer panicking that young people are too absorbed in books. We are panicking that they cannot stay absorbed in them at all.
Across 35 OECD countries with comparable data, average reading performance fell 25 points between 2018 and 2025, roughly the equivalent of one year of learning.
And I believe the scores tell us something, I’m just less certain about the story we keep attaching to them.
A score can tell us a great deal about what is happening inside the boundary we have defined. It cannot automatically tell us what may be taking shape outside it.
This does not mean that reading a long, difficult text no longer matters. It means that one capacity may be weakening while other capacities are becoming more necessary.
When text is the only way understanding counts, we risk privileging the medium over the meaning being made.
Because if declining scores merit a global alarm, surely improving belonging merits our attention.
